task: Write one sentence of your own using the word nonchalant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know nonchalant should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The bomb-disposal veteran talked about defusing mines in the same nonchalant tone most people use for grocery lists.
Relaxed just means at ease; nonchalant goes further, wearing visible unconcern about something most people would react to.
Blasé outdoes nonchalant: the nonchalant winner may be hiding a racing heart, while the blasé one has genuinely stopped being impressed by winning at all.

Unruffled means the calm is real: something disruptive happened and it genuinely failed to disturb you. The word reports your true state, not a look. Nonchalant reports only the appearance of unconcern — a nonchalant shrug can hide a racing pulse, where an unruffled person truly is not rattled.

Unfazed means not actually thrown off by something startling or difficult — the composure is genuine, and the word vouches for it. Nonchalant makes no such promise: it names the cool, unconcerned surface a person shows, which may be a careful act covering plenty of worry underneath.

The label says one granola bar packs two hundred calories of energy.
Nonchalant means appearing calmly unconcerned.
The valedictorian found out mid-shift at the diner.
Her manager read the email aloud over the milkshake machine; she nodded, said 'cool,' and went back to wiping the counter — utterly nonchalant.
Only her sister, watching from a corner booth, saw her squeeze the rag until her knuckles whitened.
Nonchalant is the exact word because it describes the appearance of unconcern, true or not: the whitened knuckles tell us the calm is a performance.
Indifferent would claim she genuinely did not care — a very different, and here plainly false, report.
Nonchalant reports only the surface: calm unconcern on display, whatever churns beneath.
That makes it the word for cool performances — and different from its cluster-mates indifferent (the concern truly absent) and apathetic (the capacity to care gone).
Casually is its adverb cousin: a nonchalant shrug is given casually.

Twenty minutes before curtain, the stage manager knocked on the dressing-room door: the lead had lost her voice, and Priya, the understudy, was going on.
The cast braced for panic.
Instead Priya kept eating her noodles and asked, between bites, whether the follow-spot operator knew about the change.
All evening her castmates marveled at the nonchalant way she handled it — a shrug at the wig fitting, a joke in the wings.
Only her roommate knew about the twenty minutes after the show, when Priya sat in the parking lot gripping the steering wheel until her hands stopped shaking.
The unconcern, in other words, had been a costume too — worn perfectly, and taken off only when no one was watching.
